title: Nvidia Slides 8% on Report Board May Oust Huang; Sensex Ends 117 Points Lower
excerpt: The after-hours fall followed a Journal report on CEO Jensen Huang; Nvidia's board said on November 8 it had no reason to believe company secrets were compromised.
body:
• Nvidia shares fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, November 11, after the Wall Street Journal reported its board was preparing to oust chief executive Jensen Huang, according to Reuters and MarketWatch.
  • The reports centre on allegations — not independently verified — involving Huang's personal relationships, including one with a woman US officials reportedly suspect of links to Chinese intelligence; Nvidia's board said on November 8 it had "no reason to believe" company secrets were compromised.
  • Nvidia had closed Wednesday up 2.9% at $173.73; S&P 500 futures slipped 0.4% and Nasdaq-100 futures about 1% after the report.
  • In India, the Sensex closed 117 points lower and the Nifty fell 41 points on Thursday, according to NDTV.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, November 11, after the Wall Street Journal reported that the chipmaker's board was preparing to oust Jensen Huang, the co-founder who has led the company since 1993, Reuters reported. Nvidia's board was meeting late on Wednesday to decide whether to oust Huang, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The fall reversed a strong regular session in which Nvidia had closed up 2.9% at $173.73 and the S&P 500 had risen 1.3%. After the report, S&P 500 e-mini futures slipped 0.4% and Nasdaq-100 futures fell nearly 1%, MarketWatch reported. Asian markets opened mixed on Thursday: South Korea's Kospi rose 0.2%, Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed 0.5% and Hong Kong shares weighed on the regional index, according to Reuters.

What has been reported — and what has not been established

The Journal reported that the board's move followed revelations of two affairs, including one with a woman US officials suspect of working with Chinese intelligence. The New York Times separately reported that Huang had a relationship with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. The allegations about foreign-intelligence links have not been independently verified, and Nvidia had not commented on the ouster report by Thursday morning in Asia.

What is on the record from the company is narrower. On November 8, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation, run by a committee of independent directors with outside counsel, after press reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. In that statement the board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security interests or confidential company information were compromised, and expressed confidence in Huang at that time. Huang acknowledged in a memo to employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, MarketWatch reported, without publicly identifying anyone.

"In that statement the board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security interests or confidential company information were compromised, and expressed confidence in Huang at that time."

The market stakes

Nvidia is the dominant supplier of the processors on which the AI build-out runs, so a leadership vacuum at the company is a market event, not only a corporate one. Reuters noted the extended-hours losses, if they held, would erase roughly $600 billion of market value. The timing compounds the uncertainty: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on November 17.

India and the diaspora investor

Indian markets absorbed the news on Thursday, with the Sensex closing 117 points lower and the Nifty down 41 points, according to NDTV's market coverage. For diaspora investors, the exposure is direct: Nvidia sits at the centre of US retirement and brokerage portfolios after its multi-year run, and Indian IT and semiconductor-linked stocks tend to move with the global chip trade. The next hard facts to watch are any statement from Nvidia's board and the November 17 results — until the board speaks, the ouster remains a report, not a decision.
